text.p: Bangladesh celebrates the 26th anniversary of its independence on Wednesday with memories of the "black night" genocide that heralded the beginning of the country's struggle for freedom.
Army, navy and air force bugles will play the last post at one minute past midnight to mark the beginning of the celebrations.
Trains and ferries will blow sirens and police bands will play at various places.

But authorities have pulled the plug on any celebrations with bright lights due to the country's current power supply shortfall, officials said. Use of firecrackers also will be discouraged to avoid accidents, police said.

On the night of March 25, 1971, the Pakistani army gunned down thousands of people in Dhaka -- then capital of the region of East Pakistan -- to thwart a movement there for independence from what is now Pakistan.
The crackdown gave birth to an armed resistance by Bengali nationalists under the leadership of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.
Mujib, chief of the Awami League, the largest political party in the territory at the time, was arrested by the Pakistani army on the same night and flown to Rawalpindi, capital of West Pakistan.

Bangladesh proclaimed independence from Pakistan on March 26, 1971, and was liberated on December 16 the same year after Mujib's followers fought a nine-month war with the Pakistani army in which it received help from India.
More than three million people lost their lives in the war, according to official figures.
Mujib, father of current Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and the first president of Bangladesh, was assassinated with most of his family in a military coup in August 1975.
Mujib's death set in motion a long spell of military rule in this south Asian country, which is plagued by poverty and frequent natural disasters.
Independence celebrations since 1975 have been low-key as military dictators concentrated on consolidating their power.
Sheik Hasina, who rose to power in a general election last June, called on Tuesday for unity and resilience as the country's needs to rebuild its economy and restore social peace.
"Let it be our vow today to build a Sonar Bangla (golden Bangladesh) to fulfil the dream of the father of the nation (Mujib)," she said in an anniversary eve message.
The celebrations will include a rally by war veterans, a cultural show by children and the lighting of the "eternal flame" at Dhaka's historic Suhrawardy garden.
Mujib first called for resistance against the Pakistani army at the garden on March 7, 1971.
Also at the garden, Hasina will also receive an "independence torch" that has been carried by war veterans across the country over the last three weeks.
The ceremony is to be attended by the presidents of Turkey, the Palestinian Authority and South Africa.
Suleyman Demirel of Turkey was the first to arrive in Dhaka on Tuesday, where he received a red carpet reception, followed by Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat and South Africa's Nelson Mandela.
Wednesday is a public holiday.
